milestones.label: Federal Circuit decision on Moderna's appeal of the Section 1498 ruling (argued Nov 5, 2026, expedited)
milestones.basis: Timing: argued Nov 5, 2026, with no decision on the court's opinions page through Nov 13. The Federal Circuit's median from argument to decision is about 3 months, and precedential opinions often take 3-6 months. The season (Nov 30, 2026 to May 30, 2027) covers roughly days 25-206 after argument. A ruling before Nov 30 is unlikely (about 0.04). The appeal raises a first-impression question of statutory interpretation, the United States filed an amicus brief, 11 amicus briefs were filed in all, and a Rule 36 affirmance is improbable. The court expedited the appeal at a party's request (Law360, Aug 24, 2026), which points to a somewhat faster ruling. P(decided by May 30, 2027) is about 0.84, which leaves about 0.80 inside the season. Outcome: the base rate of 0.75 affirmed / 0.25 reversed is moved to 0.62 / 0.38 for two reasons. (1) The United States, whose Court of Federal Claims liability would grow under Moderna's reading, filed an amicus brief supporting reversal (ECF 29), and DOJ counsel argued alongside Moderna. (2) Knobbe's Nov 11 argument report says the panel questioned how broadly Moderna reads 'for the Government', but it also pressed Arbutus on its inducement theory: 'If you are alleging inducement of which manufacturing is a part, then why should that not come within the ambit of 1498?' and 'Why wasn't that marketing conducted on behalf of the government?' A partial reversal or vacatur on the inducement claim is therefore a realistic path. Side mapping: Moderna (William M. Jay) is the appellant, which is the plaintiff side; Arbutus (David I. Berl) is the appellee, which is the defendant side. Under the March 2026 settlement, affirmance triggers up to $1.3B more from Moderna within 90 days, refundable if Moderna later prevails (en banc, at the Supreme Court or on remand). The consent judgment expressly preserves this appeal, so neither side has a reason to dismiss it before decision.

milestones.label: Fourth Circuit decision on appeal from denial of preliminary injunction (argued May 7, 2026; under submission)
milestones.basis: Timing: argued May 7, 2026, and still undecided as of Nov 14 (about 27 weeks, against the Fourth Circuit's usual 2–4 months). No opinion appears in the court's last-30-days list through Nov 13, 2026, and the opinion PDFs return 404. This case is in the extreme slow tail. Of the 62 docket numbers argued in the May 5–8, 2026 session, 59 have posted opinions; only this case and two others do not. The tail is sticky but does resolve. About 5% of the May session is undecided at 6.3 months, about 5% of the March session (3/60) at 8 months, and about 3% of the January session (2/61) at 9.5 months. That implies a hazard of very roughly 10–15% per month for cases left this late. Applied to the season (about 6.8 to 12.8 months after argument), it gives roughly 0.55–0.65. Case-specific factors pull both ways. (1) Kalshi has twice asked the court to wait for final CFTC rules if it is uncertain (ECF 124, ECF 131). The Rule 40.11 revision is expected around late November 2026, so supplemental briefing and a decision would likely both fall inside the season. (2) The circuits are now split: the 3d Cir. in Flaherty (Apr 6, 2026) ruled for Kalshi, while the 9th Cir. in Assad (Aug 28, 2026; en banc petition pending per ECF 127) and the 6th Cir. in Schuler (Sept 25, 2026) ruled against. A Supreme Court cert grant in a parallel case could lead the panel to hold this appeal past May 2027; no letter through ECF 134 mentions a cert petition or grant. (3) There is about a 5% chance of a decision Nov 16–29, before the season starts. Net estimate: 0.60. Outcome: the base rate is 0.75 affirmed / 0.25 reversed for review of a preliminary-injunction denial. Two of the three circuits that have ruled at the PI stage rejected Kalshi's position, which fits the base rate. I moved 0.05 toward vacatur because the CFTC's Interim Final Rule (effective Oct 9, 2026) and the pending swap-definition and Rule 40.11 rules (ECF 124, ECF 131) make a vacatur and remand for reconsideration plausible. That gives 0.70 / 0.30.

milestones.basis: Under the June 19, 2026 order the en banc court waits for the district court's remand ruling, and motions to govern are due 21 days after it. The district court stayed the remand on July 10, 2026 until 60 days after a CFPB Director is confirmed. If none is confirmed by Jan. 3, 2027, the parties report on Jan. 4, 2027 whether the stay should end or be extended. As of the Nov. 16, 2026 Executive Calendar, Brian Johnson's nomination (PN1079, reported Sep. 17) is pending on the floor with no cloture motion. Scenario 1 (estimated 0.6): he is confirmed by Jan. 3. The stay then runs to about Feb.-Mar. 2027 while the new Director reviews the 2026 RIF plan, a remand ruling likely comes Apr.-Jul. 2027, and the chance of a terminal disposition by May 30 is about 0.06. Scenario 2 (0.4): he is not confirmed. The nomination would be returned at sine die and could be resubmitted, so the parties may seek an extension (about 0.5). If the stay lapses, the court holds a hearing and rules around Feb.-Mar., motions to govern come around Mar.-Apr., and the chance of a disposition by May 30 is about 0.3. If the stay is extended, it is about 0.03. Total: 0.6 x 0.06 + 0.4 x (0.5 x 0.3 + 0.5 x 0.03) = about 0.10. The earliest plausible disposition is about March 2027, after the Jan. 4 report, a hearing, a ruling and the 21-day motions to govern. Outcomes: given an in-season disposition, the fastest paths are dismissal as moot if the injunction is dissolved on remand, or voluntary dismissal if a new Director changes course, so the no-merits share is 0.40. The merits share (0.60) uses the guide's base split of 0.75 affirmed / 0.25 reversed or vacated, giving 0.45 and 0.15. The case-specific evidence points both ways. For the appellees, the en banc court granted their rehearing petition and vacated the 2-1 panel ruling for the appellants (Dec. 17, 2025), and it denied the appellants' June 2026 motion to modify the stay. For the appellants, a partial stay pending appeal (Apr. 11, 2025, as modified Apr. 28, 2025) remains in effect, and the revised 2026 RIF plan makes a partial vacatur possible. The base split is therefore not adjusted. The opinions RSS through Nov. 10, 2026 shows no decision.

milestones.basis: Timing: per the guide, the Federal Circuit takes about 3 months from argument to decision, and affirmances without opinion usually come within 1–3 weeks. The two same-panel cases argued Nov 3 got Rule 36 judgments on Nov 9. 25-1616 had nothing posted through Nov 13. The case also drew three amicus briefs (ECF 41, 42, 52). Together these point toward a written opinion. Estimates: about 5% chance of a decision before Nov 30 (a late Rule 36 or a quick nonprecedential opinion) and about 13% chance it comes after May 30, 2027 (more than 7 months after argument, the long tail for opinions), so about 82% in season. Outcome: the guide's base rate is 0.75 affirmed / 0.25 reversed. It is adjusted to 0.68/0.32 for three sourced, case-specific reasons. (1) Rule 36 judgments are always affirmances, and most issue within about a week of argument. None has issued here in 10 days while two same-panel cases got one. Removing that share of the affirmance mass raises the reversal share to about 0.28–0.31. (2) The ALJ's Final ID rejected the Foxconn license defense, and the ITC's own investigative staff (OUII) agreed with Vicor that no binding agreement existed. The Commission reversed on review. (3) Two amicus briefs support reversal (Spark US Innovation; Harrison/Heiden), and LES (supporting neither party) urges requiring clear mutual assent before a patent license is inferred. On the other side, the ITC and intervenors argue substantial-evidence review of fact findings on acceptance, and the D. Mass. ruling that the POs were not offers was vacated by the 1st Circuit (132 F.4th 1), so it is given no weight. A partial reversal or vacatur counts as an appellant win.

milestones.label: Court ruling on Apple's remand proffer setting or approving the commission on linked-out purchases
milestones.basis:
Timing: the May 20 Order (ECF 1687) starts Epic's 60 days when Apple completes production. Apple projects completion on Nov 25, 2026 (ECF 1724), which puts Epic's response around late January 2027 and Apple's reply around late February 2027 at the earliest. After the reply the court 'may hold a status conference or otherwise decide the necessity and scope of any additional proceedings.' The court called this 'factfinding' and said 'this phase will likely take time' (ECF 1706). The Ninth Circuit suggested inviting expert testimony or setting up a 'Technical Committee' to determine the fee (161 F.4th, slip op. at 41-42).

Several factors push the ruling past May 30. Epic disputes whether production is complete, so the start could slip. An evidentiary hearing is possible (the contempt phase had a months-long hearing). The Supreme Court decision in No. 25-1311 (argued Jan 11, 2027) is expected by late June 2027. The court has, however, said further delay is unwarranted. On balance about 0.12 in season.

Outcomes: the Ninth Circuit allows a commission 'based on the costs that are genuinely and reasonably necessary for its coordination of external links ... but no more,' plus 'some compensation' for intellectual property directly used, reduced equitably because most of that IP already supports IAP. Apple's own proffer (ECF 1708) says 'necessary costs' so defined would yield 0%. The remedies decision is modeled as motion_granted for the prevailing side, per the guide. Terminal is false because injunction compliance and a likely appeal would keep the docket open.

In the season, fact discovery closes Dec 16, 2026, so December stays busy; motions to compel fact discovery are due within 7 days of the cutoff (Civil L.R. 37-3). milestones.basis: Under Rule 23(e) and the PSLRA, the final approval hearing usually comes ~100-150 days after preliminary approval, to allow for notice, the claims, objection and opt-out deadlines, and CAFA's 90-day period. Final approval and judgment by May 30 requires preliminary approval by about mid-January and a prompt final order (~0.15). Outcomes: the per-movant base rates (0.25 full / 0.25 part / 0.5 denied) are adapted because the motions are cross-motions on the same fair-use questions, so their results are correlated. The News Plaintiffs' motion is partial and does not end the case. Recent district-court AI-training fair-use rulings (2025) gave split and partial results, which supports a meaningful split share. activityBasis:
Current pace: 10 entries (ECF 84–93) from Aug 14 to Nov 14, 2026, about 0.77 per week. Measured from ECF 83 (07-24) to ECF 93 (11-10), it is 10 entries in 15.6 weeks, about 0.64 per week. There were no entries at all between Jul 24 and Sep 1. Using the guide's heuristic, that is about 0.2–0.23 substantive filings per week in total (about 0.1–0.12 per side) and about 0.05–0.06 rulings per week. The visible recent filings are routine: defense travel motions ECF 85 and ECF 93, and the government's speedy-trial report ECF 84 and discovery response ECF 88. Every defense ruling so far has been a grant (bond, three travel motions, two continuances).

The estimate is forward-looking because the season covers the pretrial-motion and motion-in-limine period before the Feb 3, 2027 calendar call, and possibly a trial of about 6 weeks (30 trial days per ECF 1). The rate per open week is expected filings divided by expected open weeks across four scenarios. The trial-on-schedule weight is kept consistent with the trial milestone.
(a) Trial proceeds and reaches a verdict (about 0.24): case open about 17.5 weeks until verdict; defense 1.0 and government 0.85 filings per week; about 0.3 and 0.15 rulings per week.
(b) Short continuance with active pretrial litigation in spring (about 0.20): open 26 weeks; filings 0.6 and 0.45; rulings 0.15 and 0.06.
(c) Longer continuance at roughly current pace (about 0.41): open 26 weeks; filings 0.3 and 0.22; rulings 0.08 and 0.03.
(d) Pool-defendant pleas reduce litigation (about 0.15): open 26 weeks; filings 0.2 each; rulings 0.05 and 0.03.
Result: defense about 11.3 filings over about 24.0 open weeks, so 0.47 per week; government about 9.0 over 24.0, so 0.38 per week. Defense rulings about 3.1 over 24.0, so 0.13 per week; government about 1.4 over 24.0, so 0.06 per week.

Grant rates: routine defense motions (travel, continuance) are granted almost always, while substantive defense motions (dismiss, sever, suppress, in limine, Rule 29) are mostly denied. Weighting each scenario's grant rate by its expected number of rulings gives about 0.5. Government motions (protective orders, filter protocols, in limine) are often unopposed or granted, so about 0.7.

activityBasis: Docket pace: ECF 89 (2026-07-10) to ECF 193 (2026-11-06) is 104 entries in about 17 weeks (6.1 per week). ECF 127 (2026-08-07) to ECF 193 is 66 entries in about 13 weeks (5.1 per week). Many of these entries do not score: sealed documents, filings by the non-party Chapter 7 trustee over the Rule 17 subpoena (ECF 141, 144, 145, 151, 152, 164, 165, 169, 177), pro hac vice papers and scheduling letters. Applying the guide's ~30% substantive share to ~5.5 entries a week gives about 1.7 party filings a week. The defense files more: the motion to suppress and reply, the Rule 17 subpoena motion (Sept 19) and its opposition to the trustee's motion to quash, and the post-hearing letters at ECF 176 and ECF 185. The government's visible filings are the opposition papers at ECF 124/126 and its post-hearing response. The Jan 25, 2027 trial date should raise the pace in Dec–Mar: motions in limine and oppositions, requests to charge, then evidentiary letter-briefs during trial. That supports a modest uplift over 1.7, giving 1.1 filings/week for the defense and 0.8 for the government while the case is open. Rulings: about 8% of 5.5 entries is roughly 0.45 per week, split toward the defense because it moves more often (Rule 17/privilege, bond, adjournment, and motion-in-limine rulings expected at the final pretrial conference). The suppression ruling is excluded here because it is modeled as a milestone. The defense grant rate is 0.45: its consent requests are typically granted (ECF 154 vacated a conference on its consent letter; a ruling on its ECF 93 consent bond-modification motion is not shown in the feed), but its contested motion to dismiss the CFCE count was denied on Aug 14. The government grant rate is 0.6, reflecting typical outcomes on government motions in limine.

milestones.label: Ruling on Daniel Chu's motion to suppress electronic evidence (evidentiary hearing began Oct 7, 2026; defense post-hearing letter filed Oct 16, 2026)
milestones.basis: NLR (Oct 1, 2026) describes the suppression motion as the only outstanding pretrial motion after the Aug 14 Opinion and Order. The evidentiary hearing began Oct 7, 2026 and ran three days, and the defense filed its post-hearing letter on Oct 16 (ECF 185). The court has to rule before the Jan 25, 2027 trial. The docket feed shows no ruling through Nov 6 (entries 188–193 are sealed). If the ruling falls evenly between mid-November and late January, about 77% of that period is in season. The estimate is trimmed to 0.65 because a ruling could come before Nov 30 and a plea could moot the motion. Outcomes: the defense invokes the wholesale-suppression standard of United States v. Shi Yan Liu, 239 F.3d 138 (2d Cir. 2000), which requires flagrant disregard of the warrant plus bad faith, and that relief is uncommon. However, ECF 185 at 23 states that the government conceded at the Sept 24, 2026 hearing that suppression of evidence non-responsive to the warrants is the appropriate remedy if blanket suppression is denied. That makes an order granting the motion in part (suppressing non-responsive material such as the full chat threads) more likely than for a typical suppression motion, so the split is 0.7 denied / 0.3 granted in whole or part. A ruling that only notes the government's agreement not to use non-responsive material, without granting relief, would score as denied.

milestones.label: Guilty plea by Daniel Chu before the Jan 25, 2027 trial
milestones.basis: Three former executives have pleaded guilty and are cooperating. Co-defendant and COO Goodgame pleaded on June 24, 2026 (transcript noticed at ECF 89). CFO Kollar and finance executive Seibold pleaded before Judge Liman on Dec 16, 2025, per the FDIC-OIG release. Trial is about 10 weeks away. Against that, no plea talks have been reported, Chu pleaded not guilty to the superseding indictment on June 30, 2026, and the defense is litigating actively (motion to dismiss, suppression, Rule 17 subpoenas). That places the estimate low in the guide's 0.15–0.45 range, at 0.2. The reduced-plea share is raised from 0.4 to 0.5 because the CFCE count carries a 10-year mandatory minimum (NLR, July 6, 2026), which makes a negotiated plea to lesser counts relatively more likely than a plea to all counts. The milestone is terminal because Chu is the only remaining defendant with a lawyer in our pool.

milestones.label: Jury trial set for Jan 25, 2027 begins and reaches a verdict
milestones.basis: Trial was first set for Oct 19, 2026 (NIADA, Mar 25, 2026). After the June 2026 superseding indictment, NLR (July 6, 2026) reported that Oct 19 was kept for the time being and Feb 1, 2027 was reserved as an alternative start date. The trial was then set for Jan 25, 2027, which Octus (Aug 19) and NLR (Oct 1 and Oct 21) report as current. Because the date has been moved once, the guide's base rate is 0.25. It is raised to 0.32 for two reasons. First, the court is actively managing pretrial deadlines against that date: ECF 168 flagged the time left to adjudicate privilege before trial, and the suppression hearing is complete. Second, even an adjournment of up to about two months could still produce a verdict before May 30. The estimate stays well below 0.40 because of the 20% plea risk, the unresolved suppression motion and Rule 17 privilege disputes, and the chance of further adjournment (for example, if a partial suppression ruling requires a new responsiveness review). The window assumes a 4–6 week white-collar trial plus one week, ending Mar 15. Outcome splits use the guide's base rates.

activityBasis:

Rates are therefore built from the known schedule. Sentencing is set for Jan 11, 2027 (moved Oct 7 to Oct 21, then adjourned, then reset). The case is expected to stay open about 6 weeks into the season, longer if sentencing is adjourned again.

Expected substantive filings before judgment:
- Defense: sentencing memorandum (1), supplemental or reply submissions (~0.5), forfeiture or restitution objections (~0.5), and a possible late post-trial motion with reply (~0.2 x 2). That is about 2.4 to 2.7 filings over ~7 to 8 weeks, or about 0.35 per week.
- Government: sentencing memorandum (1), forfeiture or restitution application (~0.7), possible opposition to a post-trial motion (~0.2), and other responses (~0.3). That is about 2.2 to 2.35 filings over ~8 weeks, or about 0.28 per week.

Rulings on government motions are raised to 0.1 per week, at a 0.85 grant rate. The government's forfeiture application is concrete: Beneficient's Sept 23, 2026 8-K refers to forfeiture of his and his entities' assets, and Rule 32.2(b)(2)(B) calls for a preliminary order of forfeiture before sentencing. About 0.8 government rulings are expected over the ~8 expected open weeks, which is about 0.1 per week, and such applications are usually granted.

Defense letter motions run about 0.05 per week at the default 0.5 grant rate. Rulings on a post-trial motion and on bail pending appeal are modeled as milestones and are not included here. A notice of appeal (+4 to the defense) would follow judgment, after the terminal milestone.

milestones.label: Merits decision in Anderson v. Intel Corp. Investment Policy Committee (argued Oct 6, 2026)
milestones.basis:
TIMING. The base rate for an Oct-Nov 2026 argument is 0.50. This outlook departs to 0.85 on case-specific grounds.
(1) The case was argued Oct 6, 2026, in the earliest sitting of the term. Recent October-sitting cases were almost all decided between December and May. Every OT2023 October-sitting case was decided by May 23, 2024 (Alexander v. S.C. NAACP), and every OT2024 October-sitting case by April 2, 2025 (Medical Marijuana v. Horn). There are tails on both sides: Allen v. Milligan (argued Oct 4, 2022) was decided June 8, 2023, and Mississippi v. Tennessee (argued Oct 4, 2021) was decided Nov 22, 2021.
(2) Prior ERISA pleading and prudence cases were decided about 7-12 weeks after argument: Hughes v. Northwestern (argued Dec 6, 2021; decided Jan 24, 2022), Intel v. Sulyma (argued Dec 4, 2019; decided Feb 26, 2020) and Cunningham v. Cornell (argued Jan 22, 2025; decided Apr 17, 2025). That pace points to a decision around Jan-Mar 2027.
(3) This is a statutory pleading question, not a blockbuster likely to be held to June. Argument reports describe broad agreement that meaningful comparisons matter (Bloomberg Law, Oct 6, 2026). The same report says the justices appeared torn between a narrow opinion and broader guidance, which raises some risk of separate writings.
(4) No opinion had issued as of Nov 14, and merits opinions before Nov 30 are rare, so little probability is lost before the season.
The remaining ~0.15 covers a June 2027 release (separate writings on how to define 'meaningful benchmark'), a small chance of a late-November release, and a dismissal as improvidently granted.

OUTCOME. The base rate is 0.70 reverse / 0.30 affirm. It is adjusted toward affirmance because several independent argument reports say the Court appeared inclined to affirm:
- Quarles (Oct 12, 2026) says the questioning suggested the Court is likely to affirm the Ninth Circuit, and reports Justice Kagan calling the Ninth Circuit's decision 'a pretty reasonable decision'.
- Ballard Spahr (Oct 12, 2026) says the Court appears inclined to endorse a meaningful-benchmark requirement.
- Political.org (Oct 10, 2026) reports that court-watchers saw the session leaning toward Intel.
- Law360's argument-day headline (Oct 6, 2026) was 'Justices Seem To Support End To Intel 401(k) Fund Suit'.
A residual 0.28 for petitioners covers a vacatur and remand under a less demanding definition. Ballard Spahr notes 'the Court may adopt a less demanding standard than some circuits apply', and one attorney quoted by Political.org said plaintiffs 'may lose on the question presented but still win an important limitation on the answer'.

milestones.basis: TIMING: The base rate for a case argued in Oct–Nov 2026 is 0.50 for a decision by May 30, 2027. I lowered it to 0.40 for three reasons. (1) This is a high-profile Article III / public-rights case with a divided bench (NPR: 'seems split'), and such cases tend to produce multiple separate opinions and come out in June. (2) The closest analog, SEC v. Jarkesy, was argued Nov 29, 2023 and decided June 27, 2024, and other contested November-sitting cases that term (Rahimi, Vidal v. Elster) were also decided in June. (3) Coverage (Gray TV/WCAX) expects a decision 'by the end of the June 2027' term. Window: argument + 6 weeks through June 30, 2027. OUTCOME: The base rate is 0.70 reversed / 0.30 affirmed. I shifted it to 0.40 / 0.60 based on the official transcript and on Bloomberg Law's argument report, headlined 'Top US Court Wary of DOL In-House Immigration Penalty Power'. In the transcript: Chief Justice Roberts called Oceanic Steam 'significantly different' and said the post-entry H-2A requirements 'look more like a condition of employment rather than entry.' Justice Thomas asked whether 'kicking someone out of the program' would be 'a clear way of regulating' it, then asked 'So then you can't really rely on immigration as a basis for this?' Justice Gorsuch said the government's seven immigration-statute examples 'all seemed a lot closer to the core of admission, expulsion, or deportation than this one.' On the statutory question he likened §1188(g)(2) to the penalty language in last term's FCC v. AT&T decision, which the Court read as allowing a penalty to be assessed and then enforced in court, so respondent has a second, statutory route to affirmance. Justice Kavanaugh called Tull/Jarkesy's statement that civil penalties 'can only be enforced in courts of law' 'a fairly definitive statement in our precedent'. He also called respondent's fallback line 'at war with clarity' and asked how a ruling for respondent could leave §1324 administrative penalties intact. Justice Barrett said 'the fines, I'm wondering if they're different' and said the government's best Oceanic Steam language 'can't be taken for all it's worth'. She also said respondent's fallback 'seems awfully like the government's germaneness test.' Justice Alito questioned the contract framing (helpful to the government) but called respondent's line 'kind of a hodgepodge opinion' and asked respondent whether it could win without the contract analogy. Justices Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson appeared receptive to the government. On this record four justices leaned toward respondent, Barrett and Alito were mixed, and respondent has two independent routes to affirmance, which supports 0.60 affirmed. The 0.40 for the government includes partial reversals; the government's rebuttal ('an even bigger deal would be to have a mess') asked for a clear rule either way. No scotus_argument milestone, because argument took place before the season (Nov 10, 2026).

Mann describes the respondent's and the government's arguments as 'filled for the most part with softball questions.' Affirmance credits the respondent-side pool lawyers (Hughes, Jacoby); reversal or vacatur credits McNamara. The decision ends the case at the Court.
